clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive defect of purine salvage caused by biallelic APRT variants, leading to accumulation of adenine which is oxidised by xanthine oxidase to the highly insoluble 2,8-dihydroxyadenine (DHA).

Classic presentation is recurrent radiolucent kidney stones and crystalluria, but the disorder can silently progress to chronic kidney disease and even end-stage renal failure, including recurrence in a transplanted kidney.
DHA stones are radiolucent on plain films but visible on CT, so they are frequently misclassified as uric acid stones; the key distinction is that DHA is unaffected by urinary alkalinisation.
Round brown DHA crystals with a characteristic Maltese-cross appearance under polarised light on urine microscopy are a strong diagnostic clue.
Definitive management is allopurinol or febuxostat to block xanthine oxidase, together with high fluid intake; a purine-restricted diet is a useful adjunct.
Diagnosis is often delayed for years because symptoms mimic common uric acid stone disease; unexplained crystalluria or nephrocalcinosis in a child or young adult warrants specific testing.
Stone analysis by infrared spectroscopy or X-ray crystallography, rather than routine chemical assay which may misidentify DHA, is essential for correct diagnosis.
Prognosis for renal function is excellent when xanthine oxidase inhibition is started early and maintained, underscoring the value of prompt recognition.
reference.pathophysiology: Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase catalyses the salvage of adenine to adenosine monophosphate using phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate. When the enzyme is deficient, adenine cannot be recycled and instead undergoes sequential oxidation by xanthine oxidase (xanthine dehydrogenase) first to 8-hydroxyadenine and then to 2,8-dihydroxyadenine. DHA is extremely insoluble across the physiological urinary pH range, so it precipitates in the renal tubules and urinary tract to form crystals and radiolucent stones and to deposit within the renal parenchyma as crystalline nephropathy. Because the toxic metabolite is produced downstream of xanthine oxidase, the injury is driven by ongoing DHA generation rather than by loss of purine salvage per se, which explains why xanthine oxidase inhibition is curative in intent. Two enzyme phenotypes are recognised historically (complete absence and a partial-activity variant more common in some East Asian populations), but both result in DHA overproduction and comparable clinical disease. Untreated crystal deposition provokes tubulointerstitial inflammation and progressive interstitial fibrosis, and recurrence in renal allografts occurs when the underlying enzyme defect is not addressed.
additionalDifferentials: Uric acid urolithiasis (both radiolucent, but responds to alkalinisation unlike DHA)
Xanthinuria (hereditary xanthine oxidase deficiency causing xanthine stones)
Hyperoxaluria (primary or enteric) with calcium oxalate stones
Other causes of paediatric crystalluria and nephrocalcinosis
additionalInvestigations: Stone analysis by infrared spectroscopy or X-ray crystallography to identify 2,8-dihydroxyadenine
Urine microscopy for round brown DHA crystals with Maltese-cross birefringence under polarised light
Quantification of urinary adenine and DHA (e.g. by high-performance liquid chromatography or mass spectrometry)
Measurement of APRT enzyme activity in erythrocyte lysate
Molecular genetic testing of the APRT gene for biallelic pathogenic variants
Renal ultrasound and non-contrast CT to assess stone burden and nephrocalcinosis
Serial renal function and estimated glomerular filtration rate monitoring
redFlags: Progressive decline in renal function or unexplained chronic kidney disease in a stone-former
Acute kidney injury from obstructing radiolucent stones or crystalline nephropathy
Recurrent stones despite urinary alkalinisation (points away from uric acid)
Recurrence of crystalline nephropathy in a renal transplant
Anuria or bilateral obstruction requiring urgent urological intervention
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis and lifelong xanthine oxidase inhibition plus adequate hydration, renal outcomes are excellent and stone recurrence is largely preventable. Delayed recognition can lead to irreversible chronic kidney disease or end-stage renal failure, and untreated disease may recur after transplantation.
pitfalls: Misclassifying DHA stones as uric acid stones and relying on urinary alkalinisation, which does not dissolve DHA
Routine chemical stone assays failing to distinguish DHA from uric acid, so spectroscopic analysis is required
Overlooking the diagnosis in adults, since presentation can occur at any age and not only in childhood
Failing to screen and treat before transplantation, risking allograft crystalline nephropathy
Attributing crystalluria or asymptomatic renal impairment to other causes and missing the underlying enzyme defect
